WITH tc AS (SELECT CAST(substr(week_of,1,4) AS INT) yr, employee_id, SUM(regular_hours+overtime_hours) paid FROM hr_timecards GROUP BY 1,2),
lb AS (SELECT CAST(substr(work_date,1,4) AS INT) yr, employee_id, SUM(hours) clk FROM shop_labour_entries GROUP BY 1,2)
SELECT COALESCE(tc.yr,lb.yr) yr, COUNT(tc.employee_id) emp_tc, COUNT(lb.employee_id) emp_lb, SUM(CASE WHEN tc.employee_id IS NOT NULL AND lb.employee_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) tc_no_lb, SUM(CASE WHEN tc.employee_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) lb_no_tc,
ROUND(SUM(paid),1) paid, ROUND(SUM(clk),1) clk, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN tc.employee_id IS NOT NULL THEN clk END),1) clk_matched, ROUND(SUM(paid)-SUM(clk),1) unclk, ROUND((SUM(paid)-SUM(clk))/SUM(paid),3) share
FROM tc FULL JOIN lb ON tc.yr=lb.yr AND tc.employee_id=lb.employee_id GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

# H2 notes
- q340: annual paid (timecards) flat 156.6k-170.6k; clocked falls 124.7k (2016) -> 108.6k (2025). Unclocked growth comes from clocked hours falling, not from paid hours rising. Employee sets match every year (0-2 timecard-only employees; 1 labour-only in 2023), so it isn't a population mismatch.
- q342: by role. Welders flat (0.079 -> 0.075). Rises: mill 0.358->0.545, laser 0.021->0.263, paint 0.058->0.252, brake 0.031->0.161, lathe 0.726->0.833, assembler 0.378->0.472. Inspector ~0.72-0.75 throughout.
- q345: each role clocks only to its own work centre (clean 1:1), so role = work centre.
- q343: estimated workload by work centre. Mill est h 19,811 (2016) -> 13,814 (2025), lathe 5,743 -> 3,744; laser/paint/brake roughly flat.
- q347: actual/estimate by work centre roughly flat 2017-2025 (2016 is high, probably because 2015 carry-in ops had labour clocked). Clocked hours track work, so clock discipline hasn't eroded.
- q349: within a role the whole distribution moves (p10 and p50 both rise). It isn't a few outlier employees. Some negative p10 values (clocked > paid) are posting/alignment noise.
- q351: of the 16,529 h growth 2016->2025: mill 28.8%, laser 22.5%, paint 15.9%, lathe 12.4%, brake 10.9%, assembler 10.5%, welder -2.4%.
- q354: tenured employees rise 0.327 -> 0.478 (non-welders). This isn't new-hire training.
- q358: growth priced at the 2025 median rate by role = $405,555.
Dead ends / weakeners: week alignment (annual grain gives the same picture); new hires (no); outlier employees (no); the 2025 OT stop (2025 share 0.344 vs 0.349 in 2024, no break).
Didn't test: weekly load vs unclocked share, because work_date is a posting date.

content.text:
H2 only half holds. Unclocked paid time did grow, and the growth is concentrated in particular roles. But it isn't concentrated in particular employees: whole roles moved together, which points to staffing that didn't follow the work rather than to individuals.

**What I found**
- **The growth comes from clocked hours falling, not from paid hours rising.** Paid hours stayed flat (165,056.7 h in 2016, 165,568.0 h in 2025), while hours clocked to jobs fell from 124,657.1 to 108,639.5. The unclocked share went from 0.245 to 0.344 (q340).
- **It sits in some roles and not others.** Of the 16,529 h/yr added since 2016:

  | Role | Share of growth |
  |---|---|
  | Mill machinists | 28.8% |
  | Laser operators | 22.5% |
  | Painters | 15.9% |
  | Lathe machinists | 12.4% |
  | Brake operators | 10.9% |
  | Assemblers | 10.5% |
  | Welders (the largest group) | −2.4%, flat at about 0.08 unclocked |

  (q351, q342)
- **Within each of those roles, nearly everyone moved.** The 10th percentile, median and 90th percentile all rose together, so no handful of outlier employees is driving it (q349).
- **Two different patterns drive it.**
  - **Machining:** estimated mill hours fell from 19,811 to 13,814 and lathe from 5,743 to 3,744, but those machinists' paid hours barely changed (q343, q351).
  - **Laser and paint:** workload stayed about flat, but paid hours rose by 2,504 h and 1,762 h (q343, q351).
- **The clocking itself still matches the work.** Each role clocks only to its own work centre (q345). Actual-to-estimated hours per operation are roughly stable from 2017 to 2025 (q347).

**What it doesn't explain**
- **New-hire training:** tenured staff's unclocked share rose too, from 0.327 to 0.478 (q354).
- **Week-alignment noise:** the trend holds when counted by whole years (q340).
- **The 2025 overtime stop:** 2025 (0.344) shows no break from 2024 (0.349) (q340).

**Money:** the growth since 2016, priced at each role's 2025 median rate, is **$405,555 a year** (q358). Of that, $186,428 is in machining and $151,034 in laser and paint. Benefits are excluded. The underlying level (about a quarter of paid time even in 2016) is probably indirect work, and I haven't counted it as a loss.

**What the records can't say:** what the unclocked hours were spent on, because there are no codes for indirect work. They also can't show whether it rises in slow weeks, because a labour entry's date is when it was posted, not when the work was done. Confidence is medium.

**Next step:** add indirect clock codes for mill, lathe, laser and paint, and review staffing in those work centres against estimated hours. In particular, check whether machinists could cover laser or brake work before more laser or paint hours are added.
